passage:
Monday, assembly line.
"Straight, Mridul. Sir is looking." Sumit nudged him.
"I am straight. Why do we even stand?"
"Because Sir says."
Mridul stood, mostly thinking about the ruler.
Saturday, at his grandfather's house, the radio began the anthem. Mridul jumped up.
"Nobody's checking, you know," Dada laughed.
"I know," Mridul said, hand at his side. "It feels like saying thank you. Not just a rule."
Dada turned the radio up a little.

qa.q: Who nudged Mridul in the assembly line?
What was Mridul mostly thinking about as he stood on Monday?
qa.a: Avoiding trouble: he stood because Sir said so, and he was mostly thinking about the ruler.

qa.q: How can a child move from standing for a rule to standing for a reason?
qa.a: Ask why, and notice what the gesture means to people, as Mridul did when he felt it was a way of saying thank you.

qa.q: How does Dada see Mridul jumping up for the anthem at home?
qa.a: He is amused and probably a little touched, since nobody was checking and Mridul stood by his own choice.

grounding: Illustrates a child standing for the anthem out of school obedience who later feels it as respect.

passage: Every Monday at Thabo's school in Johannesburg, the whole school stood for the anthem in the dusty quad. Thabo stood because Mrs Mokoena said so, the way he tied his shoes: without thinking. Mostly he thought about lunch. Then one Monday he noticed Diego, the new boy from Argentina, standing very still with his hand on his heart, even though he didn't know the words. After assembly Thabo asked, 'Why do you stand like that? It's not your anthem.' Diego shrugged. 'At home my abuelo taught me: when people sing for their country, you show respect. It's their heart.' Thabo thought of his own grandmother, who sang the anthem with tears in her eyes. The next Monday he stood still and actually listened to the words.

qa.q: How did Thabo feel about the anthem at first?
qa.a: Bored and indifferent; he stood without thinking and mostly thought about lunch.

qa.q: What changed the way Thabo stood?
qa.a: Diego's answer and remembering his grandmother's tears helped him see standing as respect, not just a rule.

qa.q: How does Diego see standing for another country's anthem?
qa.a: As showing respect, because the song is people's heart.

grounding: A boy who stands for the anthem only because he is told to learns from a new classmate that it is a way of showing respect.

passage: At Mohit's school, the anthem played over a crackly speaker at every morning assembly, and Mohit stood because Sir would scold anyone who didn't. His mind wandered to cricket scores. One day, Irfan's grandfather, a retired army havildar with a white moustache, came to speak at assembly. When the anthem played, the old man stood so straight and still that Mohit couldn't stop watching him. Afterwards Mohit asked, 'Why do you stand like that, even now?' The old man said, 'Because for fifty-two seconds, everyone in this country, rich or poor, stands together. It's a way of saying we respect each other.' Mohit hadn't thought of it that way. The next morning, when the speaker crackled, he stood still and thought about the whole country standing with him.

qa.q: Who came to speak at assembly?
qa.a: Irfan's grandfather, a retired army havildar.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling while watching the old man stand?
qa.a: Curious and a little moved, unable to stop watching how straight and still he stood.

qa.q: What did Mohit learn about why people stand?
qa.a: That it is a way of showing respect for each other, not just a rule to avoid being scolded.

qa.q: How does Irfan's grandfather see standing for the anthem?
qa.a: As everyone, rich or poor, standing together in respect.

grounding: A boy who stands for the anthem out of habit learns from a retired soldier that it is a shared act of respect.
